utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances for the record, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, Lisa Biersay. And I am here with STA Douglas Stringer, case manager Thomas Laugel, and our intern, Laura Stockdale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic. May I remind you that you are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that you are still under oath. Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Sorry, I appear to be having some difficulties with my headphones. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's see if Your Honours could perhaps say something, so I could test it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's definitely not working. One moment, sorry. Okay. I can hear myself, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does it work now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It does work, clearly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I wanted to start out by going back to something we discussed yesterday. This page reference is not for you, it's for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's at transcript page 11786.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I asked you -- or I said to you: "Well, Mr. Veselinovic, you said that you first met Mr. Hadzic in 1990; is that correct?" Mr. Zivanovic objected and he said: "Sorry, may we have reference where the witness said that he first met Hadzic in 1990." And I said: "Well, let me ask you the question: When did you first meet Hadzic?" And you said: "I first met Mr. Hadzic in my office in the Obrovac [Realtime transcript read in error "Opatovac"] municipality."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have -- I'm sorry, I don't have the Defence tab but it's D209, which is the admitted statement. Oh, excuse me. The transcript should read "Obrovac" not "Opatovac." Thank you. And I am interested in going to paragraph 25, which is the second-to-last page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in the English it says: "I met Mr. Goran Hadzic in 1990 when he and Professor Vojislav Vukcevic came to my house in Obrovac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would provide the witness with his statement in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What does it say in your language, where you met Mr. Hadzic in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I definitely met him at my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what -- could you read the first sentence in your language as it's written?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I met Goran Hadzic in 1990 when, together with Professor Vojislav Vukcevic, he came to my house in Obrovac." "I met Goran Hadzic in 1990 when, with Professor Vojislav Vukcevic, he came to my house in Obrovac."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the statement that you signed it says "my house" and yesterday after Mr. Zivanovic's intervention you said "my office."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my intervention as regard to the year was wrong, definitely. Just to facilitate further examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question is: So where did you meet Mr. Hadzic? Was it in your house or was it in your office?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the statement is incorrect when it says your house?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I perhaps didn't pay enough attention to this. It's implied that he came to visit me as a guest to the municipality itself, so perhaps in the translation or something -- I really didn't pay attention. But I'm certain that it was at my office. If I may --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Veselinovic. Yesterday we discussed tab 61 and we also discussed tab 63.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So respectively those would be 65 ter 6653 and 6655. And to the Trial Chamber, at this time we would tender tab 63 which is 65 ter 6655 which is the Borba article titled "Debt extortion sentences announced in RSK."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yesterday, again at transcript page 11782 it says, in talking about your arrest, you said that it was the most fatal incident in your life, and you discussed meeting Aleksandar Andjelkovic through Enriko Josif and Klara Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On the premises of the Serbian Jewish Friendship association at Morava street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Klara Mandic, was she a dentist by training, do you know? Do you know her profession?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. She had private practice. She and her sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know that she had very close ties with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did have contacts with Milosevic and with all of the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at another article.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this one can be found at tab 55. It's 65 ter 6646. And for the record, it is a VIP Daily News Report published in Belgrade, and it is publication number 87. And the primary -- the opening article is: "Messy Parliamentary Divorce Drags On." And there are other articles as well. And this appears to be dated some time around September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I'd like to direct your attention to the fourth page of this document, at the top right column. And I understand. I will read it to you because you don't read the English language. It reads --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to the first page. And the next page, please. It appears to be the -- and then the third page. And the next page, please. This is -- appears to be different than ... And if we could go back one more page, to page 3. Okay. I see. So it's at the bottom of page 3, if we could zoom in on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this comes from a section entitled: "Crime, Too Many Bosses," and the paragraph reads: "The RSK parliament in Beli Manastir suspended deputy Sergija Veselinovic, a former minister in the RSK Government who was arrested two months ago on extortion charges in Kragujevac." So is it true that you were suspended from the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been informed but it's possible that that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say you haven't been informed, I don't understand. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that as a deputy of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, I was supposed to receive in written form a decision on my suspension, or at least that they would telephone or inform me in some way or other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you saying you had no information about being suspended by the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You didn't hear about it from anyone, whether from the government or outside of the government or in the parliament or outside of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really didn't hear. I never discussed that with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You never discussed it with anyone. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Simply, I didn't find that interesting at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You didn't find it interesting that you were suspended from a position that you held with the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the incident, as I've already said, my second child was born, it had some problems with the feet, and for months we had to go for physical therapy, all kinds of treatments. I had to exercise with him three times a day, and I was completely preoccupied with that and I really wasn't interested in anything that was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to tab 61 which is 65 ter 6653. I'd like to go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at the bottom of this page, you're quoted as saying: "I am hoping for a favourable outcome." And on the next page it describes that Goran Hadzic first thought of asking you to form the Krajina government. Is it true, that statement?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? In which period?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, this is in July 1993 and you're talking about the replacement of Zecevic. So in that period.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Zecevic's appointment, Goran probably remembers this, Budimir Kosutic was there, and I was an alternative candidate for the prime minister of the government of Republic of Serbian Krajina alongside Zecevic. But we agreed at a meeting of the deputies of the SDS that Zdravko Zecevic, who had more experience with the economy, would be the prime minister and that I would join the government as the minister for culture and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So is that statement true that you were being considered?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as I have said I withdrew after the club of the MPs of the SDS met. After that, I decided not to be a candidate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to read this sentence that follows that line. It says, quoting you: "'I have heard that they have now relieved me of my deputy's seat. That can be done only by the assembly and I hope that before that I will be free and will clear up everything.'" So you had heard about efforts to relieve you of your deputy seat, hasn't you?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had one piece of information, namely that one deputy, who was called Dragan Milenko, requested that I be suspended until the termination of the trial proceedings. But there was no talk of relieving me of my post. Just a suspension and that implies a certain time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you said that can only be done by the assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The assembly with the majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And yet you said that this wasn't very important to you and that you didn't hear anything about being suspended.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really. I really wasn't interested in this at the time because if I had been interested through the club of the deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party and through the government members with whom I was on friendly terms and a great number of deputies, I could have lobbied, which is completely legitimate. But I never did that nor was I interested at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So when do you say is the end of your tenure with the Obrovac assembly?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Obrovac, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in May, April or May 2003. Excuse me, 1993. 1993 is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the end of your tenure with the RSK Assembly, according to you, is when?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, when the next elections were slated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And approximately when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, I think. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of tab 61, 65 ter 6653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to -- this is tab 54 which is 65 ter 6645.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while that is being retrieved, it is a VIP Daily News Report that we discussed yesterday. This is where --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's where I read you the language about Rade Leskovac making accusations against Goran Hadzic yesterday. Do you recall that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the second column where that figure 97.000 is, underneath that. It's about in the middle -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'll read it for you. The sentence above refers to the allegations by the prosecution in the Krusevac case against you that you used threats to recover 97.000 from a -- of a debt from a private businessman, and the next line reads: "Hadzic intervened personally in an attempt to secure Veselinovic's release." So, Mr. Veselinovic, this is another publication noting that Hadzic intervened personally to secure your release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday the Prosecution put this question many times to the witness and he answered this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear a question yet, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- there was going to be a question, but to answer the concern raised by Mr. Zivanovic, I did not put to him that yet another publication addressed the same issue that he claims he doesn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Veselinovic, it says here that Hadzic intervened personally in an attempt to secure your release. Is it your position that this article also was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My objection is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon, I spoke to my wife about this issue, and I asked her whether she remembered --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether anybody had intervened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, please. I believe you were given an instruction yesterday not to discuss your testimony with anyone, and you're saying that you discussed this with your wife and now you're going to bring that --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that that applied only to witnesses, the Prosecutor, the lawyers. I didn't know that I was not allowed to talk even to my wife about that. I really apologise. If that is the case, then I obviously made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll defer to the Trial Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I thought and hoped, Mr. Veselinovic, that the instructions I gave you were clear enough. On the one hand, I told you that you couldn't talk to any of the parties about anything, not even the weather. You couldn't have contact with any of the parties. That was the gist of what I told you yesterday. The other thing was that you couldn't discuss or talk about your testimony with anybody, and I specified not even in the street or in your hotel. And that does include your wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry. I apologise. Obviously, I did not understand your words properly. I thought that that applied only to the witnesses in these proceedings or the Prosecutor or any of the lawyers or anybody involved in these proceedings. I really did not understand your instruction the way I should have. I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to now go to tab 51, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Ms. Biersay. Sorry for the interruption, Ms. Biersay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the record, tab 51, which is 65 ter 1821.1, is an untranslated portion of what has already been admitted as P999. So to be clear, that exhibit was admitted and it was not all translated into English. So because we can't modify the already admitted exhibit, we've created this as a subset of that exhibit, and perhaps, with the Court's leave, later we can see if we can expand P999 to include this. Just by way of background for the Trial Chamber. So in -- I'm not asking that we go to P999, but within P999 this would be the B/C/S pages 16 to 17, that would be e-court pages. And at this time if we could please have the 1821.1 on the screen. And for the record, this is in October 1993 and it's an excerpt from the transcript of the tape recordings from the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina held in Beli Manastir on 9 October 1993. And if we could also have the English. We're just trying to locate the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, I see that you've been reading this in your language as that has been before you. Are you finished reading it?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now here we have a Mile Paspalj and he's asking to do the verification. He refers to: "Mr. Rade Simic from Obrovac who is the deputy of this assembly, instead of Sergija Veselinovic, who stopped to be a deputy of the assembly for the reasons that are well known to us." And there is a vote on the verification of Rade Simic. Were you aware that Rade Simic replaced you after you were removed?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I am reading it now, but I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you didn't know at the middle of the page the sentence that begins: "War Presidency ..." "War Presidency of the municipality assembly of Obrovac at its session at 27 July this year," being 1993, "relieved the duty of deputy Sergija Veselinovic, what was unanimously adopted by the municipal assembly of Obrovac at its session from 2nd of September this year."

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, either. To be very precise I didn't care. I was not interested. As I told you, as was September 1993 I definitely moved to Belgrade in Serbia. And I had almost no contacts with anybody except for my mother and father. I didn't speak to anybody on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You didn't tell anyone that you would no longer be representing the people at this assembly?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So are you saying you simply walked away from your position with the municipal assembly of Obrovac without telling anyone in May of 1993? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both as an assemblyman in the municipality of Obrovac and Republic of Serbian Krajina. I didn't inform anybody. And I had no contacts after that. I simply made that decision, and I suppose that after I failed to appear at assembly sessions they would know what to do, that they would remove me from my position in Republic of Serbian Krajina at least. And as for municipality of Obrovac, they could not take away my position in the assembly of Obrovac from me just like that because I had been elected and only in new elections could that be done. It's part of an election process. Nobody could just issue a decree to remove me from my position. It could only be done in a proper election procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Towards the end of that page, it says: "I hereby conclude that the decision of the municipal assemble of Obrovac to relieve Sergija Veselinovic from duty of a member of the People's Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina is adopted." So in this they are also relieving you of your seat in the RSK assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true for the RSK assembly but not for assembly of the municipality of Obrovac. How shall I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like European commissioners --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Veselinovic. I put it to you that in your statement that you signed that you were -- that until September 1993 you served as a president of the Obrovac municipality exactly because of this decision relieving you of your position and that's why you chose that date to put in your statement, a date you're now changing to May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I believe that it was in May 1993. September was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's also for that reason that you decided to choose September 1993 in your statement, paragraph 24, as a date that you left the RSK and went to Belgrade with your wife and your son. A date you're now changing to May 1993.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my obligations and duties ceased in May, and between May and September on several occasions for health reasons I had to go to Belgrade. I would sometimes spend ten days, sometimes a fortnight, sometimes even a month in Belgrade on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how was it that you were travelling back and forth between Knin and Belgrade so frequently?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Knin, i.e. the hospital in Knin, and the health institutions in Obrovac could not provide adequate services to my --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- child who was --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question wasn't clear. I apologise for that. How did you physically get all the way from Knin during this period of conflict, and you say a threatened aggression on the Croatian side, how did you travel from Knin to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my own car.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now ask you about Plitvice Lakes. Do you know what that is, Plitvice Lakes?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a complex of lakes with tourist facilities, hotels, motels. It's one of the most significant national parks in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Plitvice Lakes Tourist Agency?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the name does not ring a bell. However, I suppose that there was a tourist agency there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to tab 56, which is 65 ter 6647. And for the record, it's a series of articles and it -- the heading is: "Serbian and Foreign Firm Circumvent UN Embargo," and I'm interested in the last blurb -- last paragraph on the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It says here that: "As part of Yugotourist's representation, an enterprise has also been established on Cyprus that operates as the 'Plitvice Lakes Tourist Agency,' the owner of which is Sergija Veselinovic, the self-styled president of the Obrovac municipality and a member of the government of the 'Republic of Serbian Krajina.' The enterprise's co-owner is Sasa Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic's son." Is it correct that you co-owned this enterprise?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard this before. I was never on Cyprus. I never registered a company. I never incepted a company. I never signed an inception document of that kind. I never met Sasa Karadzic. And what does this mean, "the self-styled president of the municipality of Obrovac"? What do they mean when they say "self-styled"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe you answered the question. My question to you is: After you moved to Belgrade in 1993, how did you provide for your family? What did you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I registered a shop and my wife landed a job in a medical institution in Dreiser Street in Belgrade. That institution deals with the problems of various dependancies, smoking, drug using, and things like that. She worked in the legal office of that institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now you described your work with the referendum that was held in Serb majority areas, I believe, in August and September of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Am I correct that the referendum was announced on the 17th of August 1990 and held later?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very likely that you are right. I, however, do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I see that we have five minutes and I think we can address this within that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could please go to tab 59, which is 65 ter 6651. My apologies. I'd like to change the order of these exhibits. Could I get a confirmation from the interpreters if they have 65 ter 4964.3?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I apologise, we've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, before we go into the document, you said: "I see that we have five minutes" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I meant 35 minutes. I was looking at the clock, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So at this time who is Professor Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a member of the akademija, Jovo Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you are aware that he gave some speeches in the Knin area in 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there together with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I believe one of them was in Benkovac as well? One of the rallies, for lack of a better word.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, could we please play 65 ter 4964.3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We will kill Ustashas. "Thank you. Do not ask me for weapons. Don't ask me for weapons. But if weapons are needed, there will probably be somebody who will give them to you."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the information that we have is that this was on the 17th of August 1990, and Professor Raskovic says: "Do not ask me for weapons. But if weapons are needed, there will probably be someone who will give it to you." Is that what you heard him say?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this -- would you describe the crowd to which he's speaking as a very large one?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there may have been around 10.000 people at the rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this was around the time of the declaration that there would be a referendum for -- of the issue of Serb autonomy?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that corresponds to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How far is Benkovac from Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two border municipalities. Perhaps 18 kilometres. One town is next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to tab 59, which is 65 ter 6651. Excuse me. At this time we would tender 65 ter 4964.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this is an article published 20 August 1990 and its title is: "Zagreb Journalists Claim Harassed in Obrovac."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the end of that document. If we could go to the page before this one and to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And according to this article on 20 August 1990, which would have been a few days after the rally we just saw, it says: "Obrovac is still sporting the decorations that were prepared a few days ago. There is a facade of banners written in black capital letters saying: 'This is Serbia' with four Cyrillic letters S. On the road sign at the beginning of the main street which bans trucks from entering the town, the words 'and Croats too' have been added, as well as the new big slogan 'We will burn Franjo.' Two cafes which are owned by Croats from neighbouring Krusevo have been closed for several days. A broken neon sign languages above one of them and the glass has been smashed in the other so that there is a gaping hole next to Serbian symbols."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It reads: "The question would occur to any reporter: What can it be like for Croats who work here in this atmosphere, live here every day, or just drop by? They are full of anxiety and fear for their lives in their own homeland, Croatia, which is obviously not recognising them." Mr. Veselinovic, was it true that there were banners and signs as described in this article in Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see anything like that. But I remember that a cafe bar owned by a Croat from Krusevo who had returned after living in Germany, he opened a cafe bar called Zelengora and someone did break into it and I remember that some of the inventory had been stolen and that the police conducted an onsite investigation. I'm not sure, but I even think that they arrested a young man of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that there were no signs directing Croats to stay out of Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe he said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In Obrovac were there signs saying, "This is Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I heard a question, Mr. Zivanovic. The witness may answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that any posters were put up. I remember that on a rock next to the road there was a graffiti saying, "Krajina" rather than "Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So there -- according to you, there was not -- there weren't any banners saying, "This is Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He already answered the question. It is in line -- page 21, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there road signs that were made to imply that Croats should not enter into Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have existed on road signs. Even if someone had wanted to post it on road signs, it wouldn't have been allowed. The police would have arrested him and he would have been punished because it is not allowed to post any banners or anything on road signs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What about graffiti? Was there graffiti placed on signs telling Croats to stay out?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the Croats came for work on a daily basis. They came to work at the court, at the municipality, at the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions relating to Zecevic. You said that you did not want to be in Bjegovic's government. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you remained with Zecevic's government, correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But I did not accept to be a member of Bjegovic's government.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you accepted to be a member of Zecevic's government?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now have tab 5, which is P37. And just to assist, I will be going to page 58 in the English and pages 78 to 79 in the B/C/S. And I'll note this is -- these are the stenographic notes of the enlarged session of the presidency of the SFRY held on 2 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we continue, did you ever attend any sessions of the presidency of the SFRY, of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sessions of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever attend those sessions?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once in the federal assembly when we took the decision to adopt the Vance plan, I was present. Some representatives from the government of Serbia were there. I remember that Branko Kostic and Jugoslav Kostic were there. Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom of the page that appears in your language, and it says: "Mr. Zdravko Zecevic, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina government, will address you now." Is this the same Zecevic that you were talking about before?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to -- actually, in your language it would be in the next page in the B/C/S. And will you agree with me that he is talking about the possible return of Croats to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'll read this section here for the record. It says: "This issue is a complex one. The instinct made our people burn anything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes. The truth is that we cannot live together, that we do not want to live with them anymore, but there is also another type of truth which is recognised by a democratic world and which claims that these people have the right to return to their homes. I really cannot imagine how we are going to organise life then; I guess we will have to think about it later. I am picturing it like this - well, gentlemen, the schools will teach in Cyrillic, and you hate it so much that you will simply have to leave. This is what is awaiting us." So my question to you is did you agree with Mr. Zecevic that what he calls "our people" burned anything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend this session. I do not remember that speech of Mr. Zecevic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand that. My question wasn't so much whether you remembered it, but as I read it to you I'm asking whether you agreed with his assessment that "our people burnt anything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes"?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me the exact date of those words so that I could determine what happened before that and what happened later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: These notes are dated 2 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that these were villages in the area of Ravni Kotari. They were really specific in that they were mixed and there were many incidents on both sides. I'm not sure whether this number of 15.000 is correct. It seems too much to me. But I really never was focused on Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So are you saying that you don't know whether "our people burnt everything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes"?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to those areas during the war. I didn't deal with that, really. I had too many problems relating to our economy and I was fully focused on assisting our economy. The factories, the textile factory, the fabric of hydraulic cylinders, the fabric that produced stone. We had great problems to put our produce on the market. We were under sanctions, under embargo. Life was very difficult. It was difficult to collect taxes, to have any income, to have the municipal budget to pay the salaries. So in that period I was fully focused on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So are you saying that you were so focused on these issues you didn't know what was going on in other places?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that there were incidents on a daily basis, but how widespread they were that's something I really didn't know. I don't know. Perhaps Zecevic in order to depict the difficult situation he tended to glorify those issues. I think that he exaggerated. I'm not sure if his motives were political. Maybe he wanted to portray it to the people from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to convince them that the problems we were facing were difficult and complex so that he may perhaps receive some financial compensation for the renovation of houses and the return of refugees. I suppose that his motives were primarily political.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In this section that we look at he said that he was concerned about the return, right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what he would be concerned about. They wouldn't have presented any danger for us if they had returned. I think that at the time the Benkovac Brigade numbered 1400 men. We had our own police and from the security point of view they wouldn't have the represented any danger, and in economic terms they would have been more than welcome because the fields would be tilled, people would be paying taxes. I mean, I think that his motives were political or that his assessment was poor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So according to you there were no impediments for the return of Croats in economic terms or in terms of security?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself. On one occasion in the area of Maslenica at the Plitvicka Jezera motel --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you give the example, I'd like an answer to my question, which was: Are you saying, where you said that they wouldn't have presented any danger for us if they had returned, you talked about the Benkovac Brigade numbering 1400 men, "we had our own police, and from the security point of view they wouldn't have represented any danger. And in economic terms, they would have been more than welcome." And my question to you is: Are you saying that from a security point of view and an economic point of view, there were no impediments for the return of Croatian refugees?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were no impediments for their return.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we please go to tab 32, which is 65 ter 2216.2168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, while we are waiting --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- for that document, just one follow-up question for the witness. Mr. Veselinovic, what is the distance between Benkovac and Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around 18 kilometres between the two towns. But the Benkovac municipality is large in terms of its area. It reaches almost to Sibenik, Budak, Stankovci, that's that's 40 to 50 kilometres away from a Obrovac. And Zemunik Gornji is 35 or 60 kilometres from Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So there are 18 kilometres between the two towns. Is Obrovac south of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Benkovac is more to the south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Benkovac is more to the south. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 18 kilometres between the two towns. And between the borders of both municipalities, the most close borders, how many kilometres would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a place called Karin which is on the seaside, the Adriatic sea, it's Novi Grad Karin Bay. Karin Gornji is on the territory of Obrovac municipality, and Karin Donji or the lower Karin is on the territory of Benkovac municipality. But the name of the place is practically the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I understand you -- I understand it that they are neighbouring municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I fear that I would like to next discuss a document and I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There is one thing left, Ms. Biersay. You showed a document which was a translation of P999.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I thought we had to do something with it but we didn't, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right. So my proposal, and I leave it to the Registry which solution might be easier, it's either I tender it as a separate excerpt or we enlarge the already existing English translation for P999. So I'm open to guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. As long as everyone agrees, Ms. Biersay, we can just enlarge the original document. If you upload it correctly, it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is no objection from the Defence, I think that's the best course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Veselinovic, first break, 30 minutes. We'll be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for the record, the issue regarding P999 has been resolved and the exhibit modified as discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, may I please have displayed tab 32, which is P number 2216.2168. And at this time if we could go in the English, it's page 3. The section I'm interested in is the section referring to Benkovac. And I think it's on page 2 of the B/C/S. Oh, sorry, the next page, please. And it will continue on the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to the bottom of the page that appears in your language regarding Benkovac. And in the English the information that we have written is that -- first of all, I should say that this is a briefing, a monthly report for the UNPROFOR UNCIVPOL. And it's dated 2 November 1992. And it's regarding events in October of 1992 regarding Benkovac. It reads that: "2 persons were killed on the 2.10 in the village of Dobropolje. The living conditions for people in many villages in Benkovac area are very bad, i.e., Bijeljina, where about 25 Croatians have to stay out on the fields during nights, because they are afraid to be killed. "A lot of houses have been burnt or destroyed by explosives." And then it goes on. At the end of that section, it reads that: "Many of the Croatian citizen have applied to leave the UNPA, and during one month UNCIVPOL received 155 such applications." Now, Mr. Veselinovic, this document indicates that people, Croats specifically, were so afraid that they slept out in the fields at night because they are afraid to be killed. Yesterday, you described, according to you, that people were interested in leaving the territory controlled by the Serbs -- well, Croats wanted to leave areas controlled by the Serbs because they would get pensions in Croatian occupied territory. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So according to this report, what we have are people who are so afraid they don't want to stay in their own houses for fear of being killed; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report there is reference to a village, Bijeljina, and it says that 25 Croats stayed in the field. I just happened to know what was happening there. Some 25 Croats with Miroslav Usljebrka as their leader, he armed five or six of his fellow villagers. He gave them Kalashnikovs, long-barreled rifles. I know that the police searched their houses and arrested some of them. And I know that those Croats were very much shaken by that, but their fear was more due to the fact that those five or six had been arrested and they didn't know what would happen to them. They didn't fear so much for their own safety. As for the villages of Smiljcic and Kula Atalagic, it is not Alagic, Serbs were a majority and Croats were a minority population there. I don't know what the ethnic composition of Perusic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question to you is this: You said previously today that there was no issue about providing security for people in Benkovac because there were so many members of the police there. So why isn't it the case that these people were protected by that police force?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were protected. But you know what the problem was?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, before you --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: An incident would happen --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before you explain that, are you saying that these people were protected and yet they felt the need to seek refuge in the fields at night for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I was not aware that people sought refuge in the fields. Why would anybody believe that they would be better protected in a field than in their own house?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's a fair question, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could I now please have tab 33, which is P2229.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yesterday you described some events in Medveda, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medvidja?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Medvidja. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So P2229.2168. And it's the first page at the bottom that I would like to focus on. And this is a message from UNCIVPOL Sector South, Knin, and it's dated 22 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It reads: "It has also been reported earlier that about 100 Croats have left their homes in the Medvidja area and are living in the caves, fields, or forests for fear of being murdered or robbed by the local turned bandits soldiers." So, Mr. Veselinovic, this is a case of people being fearful, Croats being fearful of being murdered and otherwise mistreated. These are not people who are being motivated to leave because of pensions in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to this village, Medvidja, yesterday I said that I spoke in the elementary school whose principle was Petar Kapetanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- an ethnic Croat whose relative is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I appreciate that. My question to you is that here we have people, Croats who are fearful of being murdered, which is very different from your proposition that people are leaving Serb controlled areas in order to get pensions in Croatian controlled areas. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that there were individual incidents and killings. I told you that three ethnic Croats were killed in Medvidja, Simeon Sadarevic, a person named Erstic, and Branko Genda, they were indeed killed by somebody, I don't know who. The police carried out an onsite inspection but it is certain that they were murdered; I'm not disputing that. I suppose that in the cases of all those murders and killings, the main motive was either material gain or in the case of Simeon Sadarovic, who during the Second World War was a Croatian Ustasha, and never hid the fact, it was a well known fact that that same man had killed many Serbs in Lika and Dalmatia, which is why I assume that that had been the motive of his murder: Personal revenge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you're telling the Trial Chamber that, according to you, the Croats who are fearful of being murdered and robbed, their murders were being motivated for material gain. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know in any society, not only in wartime, things happen. For example, in Belgrade there are daily incidents, shops are broken into, people are beaten in parks and in some other cities where there are black population ghettos where things happen. There is no police in the world that can put all criminal elements under absolute control. Those who committed crimes deserve the gravest sentences. And once again, I need to repeat that the main, if not only, motive was material gain, getting hold of other people's property and assets.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to tab 41, which is P2865. And it is a document dated 12 November 1992, situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia note by the Secretary-General. And in this regard, I'd like to go to page 25. And focusing on paragraph 79. On page 25, there is a paragraph number that says ... Thank you. I will read paragraph 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this pertains to the UNPA Sector South. And Sector South, did that cover the area of Obrovac and Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And according to the report, it says: "Many people are desperate to flee the area. Yet before being granted permission from local authorities, these persons are often forced to sign a statement that their departure is voluntary, thus confusing the legal status of their property as well as erasing evidence of ethnic cleansing. UNPROFOR officials are deeply concerned over the safety of these people as well as over the reallocation and use of abandoned houses." Isn't it true that the Croats were targeted as an effort to make this a secure majority Serb region?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 70 per cent of the population were Serbs, even before the war. So it is not true -- or, rather, can I give you a specific example?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's talk about the family --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I appreciate the example, but my question to you: Isn't it true that Croats were targeted, exactly because they were Croats, for murders, for mistreatment, for robberies?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were just sporadic individual incidents. At the level of the collective, things like that were not happening. Croats were not specifically targeted as a group by another group.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now I believe that the -- Mr. Zivanovic showed you a document, P1902, which is dated 27 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could have one moment. I can retrieve the tab number, but in the meantime if we could please have P1902. I think it's Defence tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall this document dated January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you gave this as an example of an investigation being conducted.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself. The document was signed by Chief Djordje Ilic, and the officer in charge who was sent to the site was Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now go to tab 80. It should be on the list we circulated this morning. And it is Defence 65 ter 1D02617. And it's dated March 1, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're calling it up, do you know someone by the name of Nebojsa Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the assistant minister of the interior, if that's the same person, because there is another Nebojsa Pavkovic who was the chief of the General Staff of the Serbian army. He was a general. But I believe that in this case we're talking about Nebojsa Pavkovic who was the assistant minister, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to the document before you, its heading is: "Republic of Serbian Krajina Ministry of the Interior, Knin, Public Security Administration." So this would be the first Pavkovic that you described; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you can see it's a dispatch going to Benkovac SJB, Obrovac, Drinic, Kistanje, and Vrlika; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what this note says, it says: "In order to resolve the priority problems and tasks of the public security service, it is necessary to immediately start to put into effect the already prepared criminal processing of recent murders of ethnic Croat citizens, in other words, to bring the perpetrators into custody. "Since protection of the lives and property of ethnic Croat citizens has become the main security problem in all cases when such citizens express a wish to leave the RSK and state this to the," I believe it's the International Red Cross, "it is necessary to do everything to ensure that these citizens remain in the place where they are expected to stay until they leave the RSK. Such problems are particularly noticeable in Podlug, Medvidja, Nunic, Komforte and other villages. "According to reliable information, UNPROFOR and CIVPOL are preparing to set up commissions to investigate all facts relating," I believe the "to" is missing, "relating to the murder of Croats which would further discredit us in the eyes of the international community." So, Mr. Veselinovic, I put to you that the only reason there was even a semblance of an attempt to investigate crimes committed against Croats, it was an effort to persuade UNPROFOR and CIVPOL that Serb authorities are actually doing something about the problem?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard to all the murders that happened, when our police went to investigate the CIVPOL were also present. I know that that was the case in Medvidja. In Obrovac municipality, there was Serge Lazutkin and Vladimir Kononenko. The two of them usually went to investigate together with our police. When paraffin glove was taken, when prints were referred, ballistic expertise, the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina would do it together with the UNPROFOR CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we would tender Defence 65 ter 1D02617.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll be brief in the remaining time with you, Mr. Veselinovic. I would like to now direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's tab 70. And it's Defence 65 ter 1D03054. And by way of description, it's an order of 29 January 1993 from the command of the 7th SVK Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know this commander, Colonel Milan Djilas?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And just directing your attention to point 1 there, it says: "Prepare for, organise and take in (200) volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party ('Seselj men') in the area of Zegar village."

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So Seselj's men were participating in this command?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were present for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "short time," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was more than two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And they were near or in Obrovac, correct, as well?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: One group was in this place, Zegar, and another group was in Obrovac itself. They were accommodated -- as this was during the summer when the school was out, they were accommodated at the school in the classrooms. They had sleeping bags because we could not provide anything better than that for them. However, these were men who had no experience whatsoever and they did not accept to be deployed by us to units and to have our men that they would be subordinated to as commanders of the platoons, detachments, and companies. They had their own structure from the squad commander, platoon commander, company commander, to the people in charge of security. And that couldn't work at all. These were very problematic people. After a fortnight we took the decision that they couldn't -- that they were more of a burden than assistance. With regard to our own people, our own brigade, that they were not complementary. So we removed them from the brigade and sent them back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Arkan's men were also present as well? We saw on the document of yesterday that that the presence of Arkan's men increased morale.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj's volunteers, as they are called here, and Arkan's men, are not present at one and the same time. There may have been a month or a month and a half in between. Arkan's men were highly usable. That was a disciplined and well trained army. Trained for what they needed to do, mostly infiltration in enemy territory and inflicting losses on the enemy army. There were sabotage specialists, people who had received training as marines and who knew what the movements of soldiers in a battle-field meant, whereas the Seselj's group comprised of complete dilettantes, people who were unusable.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I confirm with the interpreters that they have 65 ter 4990.5, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that is tab 52. This is a time code. It goes from 21 minute and 40 seconds, and it's cut to 25 minutes and 20 seconds but I may stop it before then. Could we please play this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Actually, while we're getting sorted, did you know Mile Ulemek? Did you receive the translation? It's a question to you.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a -- I have heard it now. I know the man. I saw him once in Obrovac and another time in Knin. If that was Colonel Mile Ulemek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could please play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] 30th January 1993 the ninth day of aggression at the Obrovac front line. Still no peace. The Croatian forces either don't hear Tudjman's message on the cease-fire or they're aware of it being another deception by the international public to keep hold of the captured positions. "What do our troops say to that? "Colonel Ulemek, the commander of the Obrovac front line: Current situation is satisfactory for now. The Ustashas are not advancing anymore. There is nowhere for them to advance. We are trying to push them back and we shall definitely succeed in that, not just to push them back to their initial positions but to push them back into their own depth because we saw that those positions we left them, they are not satisfied with that. This here was Serbian and will remain Serbian forever. We came to show them that. Not to explain it or discuss much but simply to show it to them in a military manner; that is to say, the weapons have to do the work because there is no other way to deal with them. Soldiers as soldiers are good. This is the Serbian people, ready to fight. The people are a little frightened, which is normal. They have relaxed a bit as there was a sort of cease-fire for a year. They thought that the war was over for them. Unfortunately, the war is not over yet as the Ustashas do not want the peace. The Ustashas got it in their 'bungurace' rather than calling them heads that this territory is theirs, but this has never been theirs, I repeat, and it will never be theirs as long as a single Serbian soldier remains there. "The Colonel talked for a long time about the bravery ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. We can stop it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that the man you recognise as Colonel Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is your information consistent with the information that he provided in this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you have in mind, specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] 30th January 1993. The ninth day of the aggression at the Oslobodjenje front line. There is still no peace. The Croatian forces either do not hear Tudjman's messages on the cease-fire or they know in advance that it is another deception by the international public to leave the captured positions in their hands. "What do the troops say to that? "Colonel Ulemek, the commander at the Obrovac front line. "The situation as we found it is satisfactory for the time being. The Ustashas are not advancing anymore. There is nowhere for them to advance. We are trying to push them back and we shall certainly do that. Not just to push them back into their original positions but to push them into their own depth because we have seen the positions we left them, they are not satisfied with that. This here was Serbian and will remain Serbian forever. We have come here to show them that. Not to explain it or to discuss much but to show it to them in military terms; that is to say, to have the weapons firing because there is no other way to deal with them. Soldiers as soldiers, they're good. This is the Serbian people, willing to fight. The people are a little frightened, which is normal. They have relaxed for -- there was a sort of a cease-fire for a year. They believed that the war was over for them. Unfortunately, the war is not over because the Ustashas do not want the peace. The Ustashas have set a goal in their 'bungurace,' I can't call them heads, that this must be theirs, but this has never been theirs. I repeat. It has never been theirs as long as a single Serbian soldier remained here. "The Colonel talked a long time about the bravery of the Krajina soldiers who had been lacking a better co-ordinating action among their ranks but it has now been achieved. This was his response to the statement by Arkan about going all the way to Zadar. "If Commander Arkan said that be sure that he has never lied that. It will be as he says. All you have to do the choose a beach where you want to bathe. Zadar has beautiful beaches. It is now up to you to decide which one you want to bathe on. Because if he says he will go to Zadar, he will go to Zadar. That is the kind of man he is, decisive and brave, and if he sets out to do something, he will do it. In the streets of Obrovac, we met people who came from Belgrade, Novi Sad".

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the record we replayed it, this clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to the response -- his response regarding Arkan participating in an action going all the way to Zadar. Were your aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not something that the person from the video-clip said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm putting the proposition to the witness, if he's heard of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is pretty long. Maybe just this part could be repeated, just this part related to Arkan, not whole clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll be happy to read the transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Reading the transcript, Ms. Biersay, we could as well have the clip --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm happy to accompany --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see if we can find it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's more or less where you stopped the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it could be maybe read from the line 24, page 41. It is just few lines, "If commander said ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can put one simple question to the witness and perhaps we don't need to go through this exercise at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We could try that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before looking at this video-clip today, did you have information that Arkan was participating in an action to go to Zadar?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you one thing. The policy of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was defined to the effect that we would not recognise the sovereignty of the Croatian state in the Serbian ethnic territory, and we never advocated taking control of any single place where the Croats were the majority population. And secondly, Arkan's unit was very small so that not even with God's help he could have overpowered 10.000 Croats who were living -- who were at that front line with his 25 or 30 men. They were four to five times more numerous than our forces. At least that much. I want to say that Arkan had to subordinate himself to the Benkovac Brigade or the Obrovac Brigade and any operations that were taking place were taking place under the command of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the said brigade to which he was subordinated. He could not make any decisions on his own. And in particular not to take Zadar. And what Ulemek is saying here, that was more like his own personal promotion and advertising and perhaps on behalf of his unit as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Zivanovic, redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, I will ask you a few questions and I will begin with the last thing that I was interested in and that you have talked about today. It has to do with the murders. The Prosecutor asked you this. The murders of Croats, the looting of their property, and other criminal offences committed against them, and you answered that you believed that those were sporadic incidents. I'd like to know this: In that period in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, were there any murders was Serbs, any looting of their property? Were there any such similar criminal offences as those committed against Croats?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. An incomparably larger number of torched Serbian villages, livestock that was killed, as well as people. Property was torched, from crops to other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just so as we understand each other, I'm not talking now about actions carried out by the Croatian armed forces during their attacks on the Miljevci plateau or Maslenica, for example. I mean in ordinary life in the territory where the Serbs lived and the Croats lived. In addition to the attacks on the Croats as presented to you by the Prosecutor from some documents, were there any attacks on the Serbs? Were there such instances that a Serb was killed or robbed?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to clarify the issue of the time until which you were a member of the government. Do you remember if you attended the assembly session when Djordje Bjegovic as the new prime minister designate proposed and read out the list of future ministers in his government?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't attend the assembly session at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wonder if you may have participated according to what I have here --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that was on the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I object to the leading nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll use Mr. Zivanovic's words: Asked and answered. The witness said: "No, I didn't attend the assembly session at the time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would confront the witness with the -- this particular document and he will see that he was at the session but I don't know whether he was at this part of this session. I'd just like to clarify it. It is the Prosecution document, anyway. But anyway, I could withdraw this question because it is -- I could use it with other witnesses, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also showed you a document relating to a text from Borba.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been admitted as P3269.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a text written by Ljubisa Popovic which I translated to you when we met here. I will just ask you about a few details from the text and ask you to clarify them for us and tell us how correct or incorrect they are. It reads, the title reads, and I will read it to you in English and you will receive interpretation: [In English] "... a stocking on his head." [Interpretation] can you tell me whether on that occasion you or anyone who was with you wore any stockings on your heads?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely ridiculous and does not correspond to any truth at all. It's the biggest stupidity.
