utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from P3269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Is that the one on the screen and are we on the right page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I did not -- it is not on the screen and I don't know why. It was 1D2751.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist. Hopefully I won't confuse matters. But the -- I think it's the one under the Prosecution's tab 61, which was 65 ter 6653, which, in fact, is not Borba but Vreme. I know the Defence have a copy on their list as well but we have a redacted one which is probably better to use for public purposes and it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It is article from Vreme not from Borba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Where do we find the passage from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we have nothing on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. There is new one on our screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- now. So where are -- where is the passage about the stocking on their heads?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is immediately maybe seven -- eight, eighth line, there is Belgrade Vreme, in Serbo-Croatian, 26 of July 1993. And the article by Ljubisa Popovic under inverted commas: Robin Hood With a stocking on his head."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A bit lower down approximately in the middle of the text, he reads that on that occasion you were accompanied by two other persons from Krajina. From what you know of those who were present, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody except me was from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out to you another segment of this text. It's already near the bottom where it reads: "[In English] During the trial the Defence will try to prove that Sergija Veselinovic and his friends had the noble intention of collecting the debt for Tomislav Stefanovic and were going to donate to Krajina the reward for services rendered. In a news conference, his lawyer, Gradimir Moskovljevic, represented him as a Krajina Robin Hood who takes from the unscrupulous on behalf of the poor, in this case the state of Krajina." Please tell me whether you ever said or whether you know if your counsel ever said before a court that you had come to take money from the unscrupulous people in order to give it to some, for example, poor people?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It has nothing to do with what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, Exhibit P6666. It is from the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a letter that the Prosecutor got from the authorities of the Republic of Serbia in connection with this case. Amongst other things, there is a explanation of the situation. A very brief explanation. Because the paperwork of the case has been destroyed and the final decision was a suspended sentence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never served any sentences, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please. Is that tab 76 -- yeah, 76 from the Prosecution list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it shouldn't be broadcast, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's exactly why -- yes, thank you, Your Honour, for noticing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, why it could not be -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It can be discussed, we just ask that it not be broadcast on the public screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not insist on it. Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Veselinovic. That was all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Veselinovic, were you the first minister of culture and religion of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Jelic, Grnovic, was in that position before me for six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us a little bit more in detail about the reasons why you did not want to be part of the Bjegovic's government?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the Party of Democratic Change or the League of Communists of Croatia whose head was Ivica Racan and the headquarters was in Zagreb and he was absolutely loyal to Croats, i.e., to the authorities in Zagreb. In the meantime, he became an ardent advocate of the League of Communists, the Movement For Yugoslavia, and I was absolutely against such an idea. I never supported anything that had anything to do with the League of Communists and its activities. I thought that they only did harm to their own people and that they do nothing but discredit us before the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you asked to be a member of that government or to stay on your post of minister of culture and religion in that government?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bjegovic did invite me and we had a discussion. He asked me whether I would be prepared to continue working in the government. I said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was either in May or June 1993, but I'd sooner say that it was in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And last question on this topic. Who was your successor?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think I have one more thing to ask you, Mr. Veselinovic. At, I think it was yesterday, you said at transcript page 32 of that day, line 13-15: "I believe that the best solution for the states which are multiethnic and multi-confessional was to have a minority." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I still think the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how do you see that with regard to what happened in Croatia? Were the Serbs kind of a minority in the Croatian entity, something that you and your people did not accept?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were not a minority in the Republic of Croatia. They shared sovereignty with Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were a constituent people. They were not a minority population or a minority people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the risk of becoming that was a reason for you to seek autonomy, to seek independence to create your own state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the HDZ and Dr. Franjo Tudjman won in the elections, the Serbs lost almost all of their authorities. At one parliament session, as we had envisaged he would, he did that. He reduced us to the level of a minority ethnic group. So we were not longer a constituent people and we no longer shared sovereignty together with the Croats. At that parliament session, they made the decision that we would from then on become a minority people. And one of the reasons why we wanted to have our own autonomy and our personal autonomy was that. But it was just one of the motives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I have a question about something that is on transcript on page 13. That's today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. All I hear is French. I do not receive interpretation into my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] Yes, can you hear me? Can you hear me? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me? This is the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, do you hear me in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak in French now? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did not get your answer in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let us go to the transcript page 13, from lines 4 to 21. I can read that you were a member of the RSK parliament and you were suspended and replaced by Mr. Rade Simic. If I am wrong, you can correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that on the screen, but I do remember and I heard that for the first time earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay. That is exactly what I was thinking. So please tell me, did you continue to receive your salaries from the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina is where I received salaries, and those in the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Krajina did not receive salaries. They only received per diems when the assembly was in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. And now, please tell me: Did you go to the final ceremony at the end of your tenure of your mandate at the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Was such a ceremony organised at the time?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I already lived in Belgrade at that time. And since I had my own personal problems, I really didn't care much about what was going on in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I didn't inquire what was going on, especially in view of the fact that the people in power did not agree with my political positions or I with theirs and that's why Krajina ended the way it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay. It will be my last question. Do you think that it is fair to be elected to the parliament and to decide not to go anymore, even to go to say bye to the colleagues and to the institution?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had my own personal problems. I don't know if you understand what it means to have a sick child. The only thing that you can think of is that child and that child is your only goal. Nothing else matters. Politics, business, nothing. That's the most important thing that you have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I understand very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist us. You are now released as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And we wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Since this appears to be the conclusion of the proceedings for the week, I had one small matter to raise with your permission. And it -- apologies if this is already sort of in the pipeline. Next week we expect to see a fairly significant Defence witness, DGH-016, and we have yet to receive the Chamber's ruling on the motion for his statement to be admitted under 92 ter. It's a lengthy and quite hotly disputed statement, and the Chamber's ruling on the admission of the statement or whether parts of it are to be excluded, which is one of the forms of relief which the Prosecution sought in its response, would quite possibly significantly impact not only our preparations but also the length of time, for example, if the statement were to be rejected as a 92 ter statement then presumably that would affect the length of time that the Defence would wish to use for the direct examination, et cetera. So I simply raise this now to indicate that the Prosecution certainly would be grateful if the Chamber were in a position to issue its decision on DGH-016's Rule 92 ter motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Without exactly knowing it, Mr. Stringer, I'm sure that the decision is in the pipeline. But for the moment, there is nothing more that I could tell you. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The only thing I can promise you, Mr. Stringer, is that we will prioritise the decision. Just to know what we are talking about, this is a witness, the motion is for 92 ter, with an examination-in-chief of how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think what's currently envisioned is an examination-in-chief of about five hours, and that is assuming or based on, I believe, that the 92 ter statement is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I suppose so. Yes, I suppose so. As it is a 92 ter motion, it's not -- five hours is quite a lot indeed. And that would entail with a cross that will probably go over the week, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look into it. If there is nothing else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It appears that my microphone was off on page 49. 65 ter number 6666 has been admitted as Exhibit D213 under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.
